content: The systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding among HIV-positive women on antiretroviral therapy (ART) in resource-limited settings where safe replacement feeding is not feasible. The review was conducted by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and included a comprehensive search of studies without restrictions on study design. Both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies were included, provided they assessed early breastfeeding initiation (within one hour of birth), breastfeeding initiation, or exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) at three or six months. Studies not published in English were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were exclusive breastfeeding at three and six months, breastfeeding initiation, and early initiation of breastfeeding. The interventions studied included group and individual counseling, staff training, community support, policy and environmental support, and prenatal and postnatal education. Key Findings: 1. Exclusive Breastfeeding at Six Months: One cohort study (Piwowz et al., 2007) showed higher rates of EBF in the intervention group compared to the control group. A dose-response relationship was observed, where more counseling visits led to higher EBF rates. Three other studies lacked comparison groups and contributed limited evidence. 2. Exclusive Breastfeeding at Three Months: A randomized controlled trial (Tomlinson et al., 2014) demonstrated a significant increase in EBF rates in the intervention group (24%) compared to the control group (16%). Each additional visit by a community health worker was associated with a 6% relative increase in EBF rates. Four cohort studies also showed benefits of breastfeeding promotion interventions, with two reporting statistically significant results. Interventions combining individualized and group counseling were more effective. Three studies without comparison groups provided limited evidence. 3. Early Initiation of Breastfeeding (Within One Hour): The RCT (Tomlinson et al., 2014) found no difference between intervention and control groups for early initiation. A pre-post study (Mazia et al., 2009) reported an increase in breastfeeding initiation rates from 24% pre-intervention to 33% post-intervention. Two cross-sectional studies reported early initiation rates of 50-80%, but these lacked control groups. 4. Breastfeeding Initiation: The RCT (Tomlinson et al., 2014) found no effect of breastfeeding promotion on initiation rates. A pre-post study (Mazia et al., 2009) showed an increase in initiation rates from 33% to 74% post-intervention. Other observational studies reported initiation rates ranging from 53% to 95%, but these lacked control groups. Strengths and Limitations: The review included an extensive search and rigorous quality assessment of observational studies. However, publication bias and methodological limitations, such as indirectness of data, recall bias, and lack of control for confounding variables, were noted. Only one RCT was included, and most studies were observational, with quality ranging from poor to fair. Recommendations: Effective breastfeeding promotion interventions included group education combined with individual counseling, involvement of fathers and family members, community health worker support, and integration with prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs. These strategies positively impacted EBF rates and reduced postnatal HIV transmission. Future programs should focus on cost-effective strategies, family involvement, and addressing barriers such as socioeconomic factors and lack of education. Conclusion: Breastfeeding promotion interventions are effective in increasing exclusive breastfeeding rates among HIV-positive women on ART, particularly at three months. Community health worker-led home visiting models were found to be feasible and impactful. However, more high-quality randomized trials are needed to strengthen the evidence base.
